## Abstract

The length of the snout in mammals has important evolutionary consequences for the

functional systems housed within the rostrum. However, whether increased snout lengths lead

to expanded olfactory performance has rarely been examined. Here, we investigate inner rostral

function among 10 species of myrmecophagous (ant- and/or termite-eating) placental mammals

and 10 closely related species. We use non-destructive CT scanning methods to characterize

inner rostral function based on the underlying morphology of the turbinal bones in the nasal

cavity. Three approaches were chosen to address this question, including the quantification of

functional turbinal surface area, the quantification of functional turbinal three-dimensional

complexity, and geometric morphometrics. By including non-model species from several

different mammalian orders, we were able to extend the discussion surrounding turbinal

homologies to comparisons across mammals. Our results show no increased olfactory function

in all myrmecophagous species relative to their sister taxa, which suggests that there is no

trade-off for increased olfactory capabilities in myrmecophagous species with elongated snouts.

We found no evidence of convergence in turbinal morphology among all five myrmecophagous

lineages. However, we found evidence of morphological convergence in the turbinals between

the giant armadillo and the aardvark, suggesting a more complex interplay between the

evolution of turbinal morphology and ecological correlates. While myrmecophagy alone may not

be a strong enough ecological signal to overcome phylogenetic and developmental constraints,

we suggest that this might be the case at the intersection of this dietary specialization with a

primarily underground lifestyle where odorants may be difficult to detect.

Key words: morphology; turbinals; convergence; comparative anatomy; myrmecophagy;

complexity.

## Introduction

Myrmecophagous (ant- and/or termite-eating) mammals are a classic example of

convergent evolution (McGhee, 2011). They are found in five different placental orders:

Cingulata (armadillos), Pilosa (anteaters), Tubulidentata (aardvarks), Pholidota (pangolins), and

Carnivora (aardwolves) (Fig. 1). While many mammals consume ants and/or termites,

myrmecophagous species are highly specialized, relying almost exclusively on these

invertebrates as a food source (Redford, 1987). Their shared morphological features include

elongated snouts with extensible tongues, reduced or absent dentition, and claws for digging

into ant and termite mounds (Feldhamer et al., 2007). Additionally, they display convergent gut

microbiota (Delsuc et al., 2014; Teullet et al., 2023) and very low metabolic rates compared to

most other mammals (McNab, 1984). Olfaction is broadly used for prey detection across

mammals (Stoddart, 1980), and myrmecophagous species are no exception – armadillos (De

Melo & Nogueira, 2020), anteaters (Lubin & Montgomery, 1981), aardvarks (Melton, 1976),

pangolins (Mohapatra & Panda, 2014), and aardwolves (Richardson & Levitan, 1994) have all

been documented making food choices while exhibiting sniffing behaviors. Despite similar snout

morphologies and sniffing behaviors during predation, the internal anatomy of the olfactory

system has never been investigated in a comparative phylogenetic framework for

myrmecophagous mammals.

The nasal cavity of mammals is arranged as a tripartite capsule consisting of three

regions defined by their location along the lateral wall during fetal morphogenesis: the pars

anterior, the pars intermedia, and the pars posterior (Maier, 1993; Maier & Ruf, 2014; Martinez,

Courcelle, et al., 2023; Ruf, 2020; Smith & Rossie, 2008). In each of these regions, cartilaginous

precursors ossify into bones called turbinals. In adults, turbinals range in morphology from

small, thin plates of bone to interweaving, paper-thin filigreed scrolls (Hillenius, 1992; Martinez,

Okrouhlík, et al., 2023; Rowe et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2021). While there is disagreement


<!-- Page 5 -->


regarding the specific terminology used to describe individual turbinals (see Macrini 2012; Ruf

2014; Wagner and Ruf 2019; Lundeen and Kirk 2019; Martinez, Amson, et al. 2023 for a deeper

discussion), they can broadly be categorized into two distinct functional types (Green et al.,

2012; Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Martinez et al., 2018, 2020; Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al.,

2023; Valkenburgh et al., 2011; Wagner & Ruf, 2019). The more anterior turbinals, which are

involved in respiratory function, are covered with non-sensory epithelium that filters, warms, and

humidifies air before it reaches the lungs (Jackson & Schmidt-Nielsen, 1964; Schmidt-Nielsen et

al., 1970; Yee et al., 2016). The more posterior turbinals, which are involved in olfactory

function, are covered with sensory epithelium that binds odorants circulating the nasal cavity

and communicates sensory information to the olfactory bulb for processing (Purves et al., 2001;

Smith et al., 2011; Smith & Bonar, 2022; Yee et al., 2016). Due to this variation in turbinal

function, different selective pressures may influence turbinal morphology throughout the nasal

cavity.

Respiratory turbinals evolved mainly in response to thermoregulatory demands (Schmidt-

Nielsen et al., 1970). Because water conducts heat away from the body more quickly than air,

transitions to more aquatic lifestyles require greater thermoregulatory control (Martinez, Amson,

et al., 2023; Martinez et al., 2020; Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al., 2023; Valkenburgh et al., 2011).

Aquatic mammals have long been described as having massively complex respiratory turbinals

(Mason et al., 2020; Negus, 1956), and recent research in carnivorans (Valkenburgh et al.,

2011) and more broadly across different mammal clades (Martinez et al., 2020; Martinez,

Okrouhlík, et al., 2023) has confirmed significantly increased respiratory turbinal surface area in

aquatic and amphibious mammals, which may correspond to greater capacity for respiratory

function. A similar effect might be expected across a latitudinal gradient, but published results to

date are less straightforward. A study comparing 20 caniform carnivoran species found no

significant differences in respiratory turbinal size associated with latitude (Green et al., 2012).


<!-- Page 6 -->


However, comparisons of three individual sister taxa within the same study showed greater total

turbinal surface area (both respiratory and olfactory turbinals) and chamber volume in Arctic

species compared to more temperate ones, demonstrating the complex interplay of the many

factors that influence turbinal morphology. Diet is an example of a factor that interacts with the

environment in complex ways in terms of how it influences turbinal morphology. Olfactory

turbinals are known to be associated with prey detection and are therefore influenced directly by

diet. Large terrestrial carnivores that forage in widely dispersed habitats have expanded

olfactory turbinal surface areas, which may help in the detection of odors over large distances or

at low concentrations (Green et al., 2012; Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Martinez, Courcelle, et

al., 2023; Pihlström et al., 2005; Valkenburgh et al., 2011). Aquatic mammals that forage

underwater instead have a reduced olfactory turbinal surface area, which likely reflects a

reduced reliance on olfaction to find prey in aquatic environments (Martinez, Courcelle, et al.,

2023; Martinez et al., 2020; Valkenburgh et al., 2011). These studies demonstrate how both the

environment and dietary specialization must be considered in testing the potential adaptations

of turbinals.

In addition to distribution of sensory epithelium, the morphology of the inner nasal cavity

has been demonstrated to influence airflow and potentially olfactory performance in dogs

(Craven et al., 2007, 2010), cats (Pang et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2023), bats (Eiting et al., 2015),

and strepsirrhine primates (Smith et al., 2019). Broadly, the effect of internal morphology is

thought to slow down airflow to improve absorption of odorants in contact with olfactory mucosa,

which may help in overall olfactory capability without modifying total surface area. Despite this

functional explanation, comparative airflow dynamics in an ecological context are limited and

suggest that selection for other demands on the snout, such as breathing and feeding, may

override adaptive changes to airflow dynamics (Eiting et al., 2015). An alternative hypothesis

could be that developmental changes that adaptively influence airflow dynamics are more


<!-- Page 7 -->


difficult to produce than simply increasing the overall surface area of turbinals, and thus it may

be a less common evolutionary path towards increased olfactory capability.

Here, we micro-CT scanned the skulls of ten myrmecophagous (anteaters, pangolins,

aardvarks, pangolins, and aardwolves) and ten non-myrmecophagous (sister taxa) placental

species (Fig. 1) to investigate whether the convergent evolution towards myrmecophagy

included similar changes in turbinal morphology. We use multiple approaches for quantifying

turbinals including direct surface area measurements, geometric morphometrics, and 3D

complexity (Martinez et al., 2018). Myrmecophagous mammals need to detect highly specific

odorants that may be concentrated deep within ant and termite mounds (Ocko et al., 2019). We

hypothesize that these species will have well-developed olfactory turbinals to aid in prey

detection. In addition to diet, turbinal morphology is constrained by morphological factors, and

snout length in mammals has important evolutionary consequences for the functional systems

housed within the rostrum. Feliform carnivorans have reduced snouts and display reduced

olfactory turbinal surface areas (Valkenburgh et al., 2014), though computational fluid dynamics

simulations suggest feliforms are still highly capable of efficient odorant detection (Wu et al.,

2023), suggesting that constraints due to changes in overall snout morphology and size may

alter how olfactory function is maintained throughout evolution. In contrast, whether a

subsequent increase in snout length is associated with expanded olfactory turbinal surface area

and complexity has rarely been properly investigated in other mammalian groups (see Martinez

et al. 2018), and myrmecophagous species provide an ideal system to investigate this question.

## Materials and Methods

Biological Samples

The materials sampled in this project belong to the collections at the Natural History

Museum in London (NHMUK, London, United Kingdom), the Muséum National d’Histoire

Naturelle (MNHN, Paris, France), the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology (MVZ, Berkeley, CA,

United States), the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH, New York, United States), the

Koninklijk Museum voor Midden-Afrika (KMMA, Tervuren, Belgium), the Institut Royal des

Sciences Naturelles de Belgique (IRSNB, Bruxelles, Belgium), and the University of Montpellier

(UM, Montpellier, France). The dataset is composed of 33 museum specimens (20 species) of

myrmecophagous placentals (anteaters, giant armadillos, aardvarks, pangolins, and

aardwolves) as well as closely related species (Table 1). For each of the following species,

multiple individuals were analyzed to explore intraspecific variation in turbinal morphology:

Cyclopes didactylus (n = 4), Myrmecophaga tridactyla (n = 2), Tamandua tetradactyla (n = 4),

Tamandua mexicana (n = 4), Phataginus tetradactyla (n = 2), Smutsia gigantea (n = 2), and

Proteles cristatus (n = 2). All collected specimens were adults except for one juvenile T.

tetradactyla (NHMUK-75-1369) and one juvenile S. gigantea (MNHN-1913-113).

The phylogenetic relationships of the 20 focal species (Fig. 1) have been reconstructed

based on complete mitochondrial genomes aligned using MAFFT v7 (Katoh & Standley, 2013)

using Maximum Likelihood with RAxML v8 (Stamatakis, 2014) under the GTR+G model. The

complete mitochondrial genome was unavailable for Tenrec ecaudatus, so only the 12S rRNA,

Val-tRNA, 16S rRNA, and ND2 genes were used. Divergence dates were inferred using the

RelTime method (Tamura et al., 2012) based on three fossil calibration constraints: Placentalia

at 105 Million years ago (Mya), Xenarthra at 65 Mya, and Carnivora at 55 Mya (Puttick et al.,

2016).

Micro-Computed Tomography Scans

X-ray micro-computed tomography (µCT) scans were produced for each specimen using

the SkyScan 1076 (ISEM, Montpellier) or the Nikon Metrology HMX ST 225 (NHMUK, London,

United Kingdom). The voxel size for each scan was recorded in Table 1. Three-dimensional

reconstructions were performed in AVIZO v. 9.4.0 software (Visualization Sciences Group,

Burlington, MA, USA). For each specimen, turbinals in the left side of the nasal cavity were

segmented by manually selecting and delimiting individual turbinals slice by slice (2-

Dimensional selection) (Fig. 2). In one of the T. tetradactyla specimens, the left maxilloturbinal

was broken, so the right maxilloturbinal was used instead. For each turbinal, three-dimensional

surface meshes were generated to measure surface area, calculate three-dimensional

complexity, and compare using geometric morphometrics, following Martinez et al. (2018). All

3D reconstructions were deposited in MorphoMuseum (Wright et al. 2024).

Anatomical Terminology

As parts of the internal nasal skeleton, turbinals ossify from three chondrification centers:

the pars anterior, the pars intermedia, and the pars posterior (Maier, 1993; Maier & Ruf, 2014;

Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Ruf, 2020; Smith & Rossie, 2008). The maxilloturbinal is a medial

attachment to the maxilla that develops from the ventral margin of the paries nasi (Macrini,

2012). The nasoturbinal and semicircular lamina (= lamina semicircularis) form a compound

structure consisting of two components that develop from a ventral folding of the tectum and a

lateral folding of the pars anterior, respectively (Macrini, 2012; Smith & Rossie, 2006) – in some

adults, these two structures can be difficult to distinguish and appear as merged into one

ossified element. The endoturbinals include turbinals in the ethmoturbinal recess that develop


<!-- Page 10 -->


as folds of the pars posterior, stretch to the midline of the nasal cavity, and coalesce

rostroventrally to form the ethmoid plate, which, with the vomer, makes up the posterior

transverse lamina (Macrini, 2012; Rowe et al., 2005). Finally, the ectoturbinals include any

turbinal that attaches between the nasoturbinal and the first endoturbinal and develops as a fold

of the pars intermedia (Allen, 1882; Macrini, 2012). In this study, all turbinals that ossify in the

recessus frontoturbinalis are called frontoturbinals; all turbinals that ossify in the recessus

ethmoturbinalis are called ethmoturbinals; interturbinals ossify in the spaces between already-

ossified frontoturbinals and ethmoturbinals (Maier & Ruf, 2014; Paulli, 1900; Voit, 1909). When

studying turbinal homologies, structures should ideally be classified using developmental series

(Macrini et al., 2023). However, many extant vertebrate species, including all species

investigated here, do not have growth series available to study. Pending future developmental

studies, we consider the frontoturbinals to be equivalent to ectoturbinals, ethmoturbinals to be

equivalent to endoturbinals, and interturbinals included in the former or latter depending on

location.

The interturbinals may be incorrectly described in adult specimens as frontoturbinals or

ethmoturbinals (Maier, 1993; Maier & Ruf, 2014; Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Rowe et al.,

2005). These interturbinals are mostly found in the olfactory recess of the rostrum (but see also

Martinez et al. 2020; Martinez, Amson, et al. 2023 for interturbinals elsewhere). Hypotheses on

turbinal homology can be straightforward in mammals with relatively simple turbinals such as

rodents, lagomorphs, bats and Eulipotyphla (e.g., Ruf 2014; 2020; Martinez et al. 2018; 2020;

Martinez, Amson, et al. 2023; Ito et al. 2021; T. D. Smith and Bonar 2022). However, such

hypotheses were more difficult to make in carnivorans (but see Wagner and Ruf 2019) and most

of the myrmecophagous placental mammals studied here, which sometimes developed

numerous fronto-, inter- and ethmoturbinals. In this study, the colors of the segmented turbinals

aim to propose turbinal correspondence between species (see Martinez, Amson, et al. 2023).

Frontoturbinals and ethmoturbinals are considered to be serially homologous and are

traditionally numbered from anterodorsal to posteroventral (Allen, 1882; Macrini, 2012, 2014;

similarly indistinguishable except for ethmoturbinal I, which can be identified by its anterior

protrusion alongside the maxilloturbinal. Because the remaining ethmoturbinals and

frontoturbinals cannot be distinguished sequentially in all the species studied here, they are not

numbered under assumptions of serial homology (Macrini, 2012; Macrini et al., 2023).

Functional Turbinal Divisions

From the literature, it appears that the maxilloturbinal is primarily covered in respiratory

mucosa across a wide taxonomic range while the frontoturbinals and most of the ethmoturbinals

are primarily covered in olfactory epithelium (Green et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2011; Valkenburgh

et al., 2011, 2014). However, histological stains of Monodelphis and Microcebus demonstrate

that the nasoturbinal and ethmoturbinal I contain at least some degree of both respiratory and

olfactory epithelium (Rowe et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2011).

In determining functional divisions for surface area and complexity comparisons, we

compared three approaches: (1) the maxilloturbinal was classified as respiratory, while the rest

of the turbinals (nasoturbinal, frontoturbinals, ethmoturbinals) were classified as olfactory

Geometric Morphometrics

For each specimen, 19 homologous 3D landmarks were placed on the reconstructed

models of turbinals (Table 4, Fig. 2) using Avizo software (VSG Inc., Burlington, MA, USA).

Generalized Procrustes analysis was performed on the coordinate data to obtain shape

variables (Adams & Otárola�Castillo, 2013; Goodall, 1991) using the “geomorph” package

(Adams et al., 2022) in R version 3.5.0 (R Core Team, 2024). This method of generalized least-

squares superimposition aligns all landmark configurations by optimally rotating, translating to

the origin, and scaling to centroid size for each specimen. A multivariate analysis of variance

(MANOVA) was performed on the principal component (PCA) scores that explained 90% of the

variance to test for the effects of diet and phylogenetic order on turbinal shape using the

“RRPP” package in R (Collyer & Adams, 2018). Additionally, Bloomberg’s K (n = 10,000

simulations) (Bloomberg et al., 2003) and Pagel’s lambda (Pagel, 1999) were calculated using

the “phytools” package in R (Revell, 2012).

Turbinal Complexity

We divided turbinal complexity into three qualitative types that exist along a spectrum of

turbinal diversity: Type I - turbinals are considerably spaced and do not intertwine with other

turbinals; Type II - turbinals are minimally spaced and may slightly intertwine with other

turbinals; Type III - the turbinals are minimally spaced and heavily intertwine with other turbinals.

3D complexity measurements for each turbinal were performed in MorphoDig (Lebrun & Orliac,

2016). A convex hull, or the smallest convex set of points that contains the object in Euclidean

space, was created for each turbinal. 3D complexity is a dimensionless metric and was defined

as the area ratio between the surface area of the turbinal and the surface area of the

encompassing convex hull (Martinez et al., 2018).

Functional divisions of turbinals for 3D complexity measurements are as follows:

respiratory complex - the maxilloturbinal; and olfactory complex - the ethmoturbinals (except for

ethmoturbinal I) and the frontoturbinals. The nasoturbinal and ethmoturbinal I were excluded

here to avoid partitioning three-dimensional objects into uninformative subsets as they both

contain at least some degree of each respiratory and olfactory epithelium (Martinez, Amson, et

al., 2023; Martinez et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2016; Ruf, 2022; Smith et al., 2007, 2016; Yee et

al., 2016). Respiratory turbinal complexity therefore is equivalent to the complexity of the

maxilloturbinal, and olfactory turbinal complexity is calculated by taking the average complexity

for the ethmoturbinals (not including ethmoturbinal I) and the frontoturbinals.

Statistical Comparisons

The relationship between logged olfactory and respiratory turbinal surface area and

complexity was investigated using the ‘contMap’ function from the ‘phytools’ package (Revell,

2024) in R (R Core Team, 2024). Analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were calculated to test for


<!-- Page 15 -->


differences in olfactory and respiratory turbinal surface area and complexity according to dietary

specialization. Additionally, ANOVAs were performed to test for differences in the ratio between

olfactory and respiratory turbinal surface area and complexity, respectively. To account for the

species’ shared evolutionary history, phylogenetic analyses of covariance (ANCOVA) were

performed on total, respiratory, and olfactory turbinal surface area relative to two measures of

body size (body mass and skull length) with dietary specialization defined as a factor in each

model. The phylogenetic ANCOVAs were performed using the ‘gls’ function from the ‘nlme’

package, which allows the specified phylogeny to influence the correlation structure of the

residual error (Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).

## Results

Morphological Variation in Turbinals

Reconstructed models for each species are shown in Figs. 3-7 and, in more detail, in the

Supplementary Materials. Within the nasal cavity of most species we observed, the general

case for each turbinal is that the position tends to mirror the direction of the snout (through the

text, we use the term “snout” to refer solely to the osteological portion of this region, while

recognizing that the proper anatomical structure also includes soft tissue components such as

cartilage). They are elongated rostrocaudally, exhibiting fractal-like, branching spirals along this

axis. Occasionally, the ethmoturbinals and frontoturbinals among the species examined here

are rotated about their mediolateral axis so that they are no longer parallel with the

maxilloturbinal and nasoturbinal rostrocaudally. The semicircular lamina contains a wing-like

lateral protrusion called the uncinate process. It forms the rostroventral border of the lateral

recess in most of the species we observed. Considerable intraspecific variation exists in

ethmoturbinal and frontoturbinal count (Table 5). The only exception to this variation is Cy.


<!-- Page 16 -->


didactylus (n = 4), consistently displaying four ethmoturbinals and two frontoturbinals (Table 5).

Most turbinals exhibit Type I complexity, meaning they do not interweave and have considerable

space between them. Type II complexity describes the maxilloturbinals and rostral portions of

ethmoturbinal I in most of the Carnivora, while Type III complexity describes uniquely the

ethmoturbinals and frontoturbinals of P. maximus and O. afer. In the following sections, each

turbinal is described in more detail from a comparative perspective, highlighting the major

features that differ among the species segmented in this study.

Maxilloturbinal

In all specimens, the maxilloturbinal spans approximately from the rostral opening of the

nasal cavity to the semicircular lamina, positioned ventrolaterally to the nasoturbinal. The

maxilloturbinal is the most rostral turbinal in both sloth species (Fig. 3A-B), both Dasypus

species (Fig. 4A-B), all five species of Carnivora and M. culionensis (Figs. 5, 6 and S1), E.

rozeti (Fig. S1) O. afer and T. ecaudatus (Figs. 7 and S1). The opposite condition is observed in

the two pangolin species S. gigantea and P. tetradactyla.

The maxilloturbinal is arbor-like in shape, except for two cases: (1) in D. novemcinctus

(Fig. 4A) and D. pilosus (Fig. 4B), it is elongated rostrocaudally and pointed at the rostral end,

and (2) in B. tridactylus (Fig. 3A) and Ch. Didactylus (Fig. 3B), it is elongated along its

ventrodorsal axis. B. tridactylus (Fig. 3A) has a particularly unique maxilloturbinal, shaped

triangularly along a rostrocaudal axis with the apex pointing ventrally and divided into two parts

posteriorly. In D. novemcinctus, the maxilloturbinal is integrated to the skull posteriorly. The

maxilloturbinal typically exhibits a single scroll but can also contain two or three branches (as in

P. maximus and O. afer) or many bifurcating branches (as in V. vulpes and A. lagopus). Most

often, the maxilloturbinal exhibits Type I complexity. Only F. silvestris (Fig. S1), A. lagopus (Fig.

S1), and V. vulpes (Fig. 6A) exhibit Type II complexity, with the caudal part of the maxilloturbinal

The semicircular lamina is an ethmoidal structure that is continuous and ossified with the

nasoturbinal in 19 of the 20 species in this study and shows the most variation in shape among

uncinate process is reduced rostrocaudally (Figs. 3A and S1). The orientation of this lateral

expansion is almost directly lateral from the midline of the nasal septum but can also be rotated

Geometric Morphometrics

A principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that 90% of the variation in turbinal shape

was explained by the first nine (out of 21) principal components (PCs). The first two PCs

explained 49.5% of the total variance. In this morphospace (Fig. 8), myrmecophagous species

only display slightly larger values along PC1 and PC2 compared to non-myrmecophagous

species. In general, the myrmecophagous species display varied turbinal morphologies (Fig. 8).

The pangolins sit in the middle of the morphospace, alongside C. didactylus. In contrast, the

turbinals of the anteaters and the giant armadillo (P. maximus) occupy positive values of PC1

and PC2, corresponding to elongation of the snout and a slightly more caudal maxilloturbinal,


<!-- Page 25 -->


respectively. The turbinals of the aardvark (O. afer) clearly depart from this group showing the

maximum positive values on PC2, which mainly express differences in height of the

maxilloturbinal along the ventrodorsal axis. The turbinals of the southern aardwolf (Proteles

cristatus) evolved towards the maximum values of PC2 and the minimum values of PC1, and

are characterized by elongated and mediolaterally rotated maxilloturbinal. A multivariate

analysis of variance (MANOVA) found that variation in turbinal shape was explained by both

dietary specialization (p = 0.023) and taxonomic order (p = 0.001), though the latter explained

most of the variance in the model (r2 = 0.576 compared to 0.101 for diet). Further, the resulting

morphospace indicates that separation by diet, though significant, is minimal (Fig. 8).

Bloomberg’s K (0.451) and Pagel’s lambda (0.133) both suggest a departure from a Brownian

motion explanation of evolution that could be in part explained by convergence, though neither

test was statistically significant (p > 0.05).

A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) found no significant differences in turbinal

## Discussion

Turbinal Homology

By including non-model species from several different mammalian orders, we were able

to extend the discussion surrounding turbinal homologies to comparisons across mammals (

Macrini 2012; Ruf 2014; Macrini et al. 2023; Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al. 2023; Martinez, Amson,

et al. 2023). Under the hypothesis of serial homology, previous research has typically used a

relative position numbering system to compare individual turbinals between different species

(e.g., Macrini 2014). There are two major complications with this approach. First, in some cases

it is not possible to number ethmoturbinals and frontoturbinals by relative position. The

ethmoturbinals and frontoturbinals of P. maximus, D. novemcinctus, D. pilosus, and O. afer are

interwoven with overlapping attachments to the cribriform plate and posterior transverse lamina.

These turbinals are not positioned in an obvious sequential order for consistent numbering.

Ordering the turbinals from anterodorsal to posteroventral in these species will yield a different

sequence depending on whether counting is conducted closer to the posterior transverse lamina

or closer to the cribriform plate. The second complication with this approach is that

interturbinals, which ossify in the spaces between existing frontoturbinals or ethmoturbinals

(Maier and Ruf 2014b; Ruf, 2014; Martinez et al. 2018, 2023c), are often not easily

distinguished from surrounding turbinals in adult specimens. In some cases, such as non-model

or fossil species, adult skulls are the only material available for study. As a result, serial

homology is not a practical approach for interspecific comparisons and deep-time studies of

turbinal evolution at the mammalian taxonomic scale.

Ridges on the inner surface of the nasal and maxillary bones have been identified in non-

mammalian therapsids, indicating the presence of ossified turbinals prior to the origin of

mammals (Hillenius 1992; Hillenius and Ruben 2004 but see Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al. 2023). A


<!-- Page 27 -->


current hypothesis for the number of ancestral ethmoturbinals in placentals includes four

ethmoturbinals (Macrini, 2014; Moore, 1981). This count considers the pars anterior and

posterior of the ethmoturbinal I (Fig. 2) as distinct turbinals. Previous research has identified

four ethmoturbinals as well in fetal mouse lemurs, tenrecs, voles, and flying lemurs (Smith and

Rossie, 2008). Macrini (2014) further suggested that the so-called endoturbinal III (not

equivalent to the ethmoturbinal III here) in the marsupials Caluromys philander and

Monodelphis domestica is an interturbinal and may have been lost in the placental lineage

(Macrini, 2014). In general, factors influencing turbinal number appear to be clade-specific and

might depend on the specific evolutionary constraints applying to each group (e.g., Martinez,

Amson, et al. 2023). Our findings demonstrate considerable intraspecific and interspecific

variation in the number of turbinals (Table 5), suggesting a greater plasticity than previously

assumed. However, some trends are noticeable, ethmoturbinals are usually more numerous

than frontoturbinals, with only a few exceptions (M. tridactyla, O. afer, V. vulpes, and A.

lagopus). The relative number of ethmo- and frontoturbinals usually does not differ markedly,

except that sloths have an unusually low number of frontoturbinals compared to ethmoturbinals.

We also observed that the number of interturbinals increases with the overall number of ethmo-

and frontoturbinals, and that this number is always higher in the most numerous type of

turbinals (either ethmo- or frontoturbinals). Pangolins consistently display a higher number of

ethmoturbinals compared to their carnivoran sister taxa (Table 5). The aardvark O. afer also

presents a much higher ethmoturbinal number when compared to its sister taxa (T. ecaudatus

and E. rozeti). These two cases could be intuitively linked to an adaptation to a

myrmecophagous diet, but we showed that the number of turbinals within Pilosa does not follow

a similar pattern (Table 5), with the giant anteater M. tridactyla being the only myrmecophagous

pilosan exhibiting larger ethmoturbinal and frontoturbinal numbers. Such differences might

suggest that differences in turbinal number might simply be taxon-specific and linked to spatial

and developmental constraints. Within a clade, we also observed that larger species tend to


<!-- Page 28 -->


present higher ethmoturbinal and frontoturbinal counts, suggesting that turbinal number might

also be related to body size (see Valkenburgh et al. 2014).

Turbinal Function

Mapping turbinal morphology to function has been an active area of research over the

past two decades due to advancements in non-destructive scanning technologies (Joeckel et

al., 2003; Rowe et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2004). Many studies have focused primarily on turbinal

surface area as this metric is assumed to represent the total amount of epithelium lining each

turbinal and may serve as a direct functional proxy (Valkenburgh et al. 2011; Green et al. 2012;

Yee et al. 2016; Lundeen and Kirk 2019; Wagner and Ruf 2019; Martinez et al. 2018; Melin et

al. 2022; Martinez et al. 2020; Martinez, Courcelle, et al. 2023; Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al. 2023,

but see Martinez, Amson, et al. 2023). In this study, we grouped turbinals into morphological

units (respiratory and olfactory complexes) and compared traits for each grouping among

different species. Regarding functional turbinal classification, Green (2012) previously referred

to the maxilloturbinal as respiratory and all other turbinals as olfactory. Ruf (2014) grouped the

frontoturbinals and ethmoturbinals together as olfactory. Histological staining of M. murinus

revealed 96% coverage of the nasoturbinal surface with olfactory epithelium (Smith et al., 2011).

A histological stain of M. domestica showed that the apical surface of the nasoturbinal is

primarily covered with olfactory epithelium, while the walls of the superior recess and maxillary

sinus, the inferior surface of ethmoturbinal I, and the surface of the nasoturbinal facing away

from the nasal lumen were lined with respiratory epithelium  (Barrios et al., 2014; Harkema et

al., 2006; Rowe et al., 2005). The rostral extension of ethmoturbinal I in felids has also been

proposed to contain respiratory epithelium instead of olfactory epithelium to account for a

shortened snout (Valkenburgh et al., 2014). Overall, the epithelial cover of the naso- and

ethmoturbinal I greatly varies between species (e.g., T. D. Smith et al. 2004; T. D. Smith, Eiting,


<!-- Page 29 -->


and Rossie 2011; T. D. Smith and Rossie 2008; Yee et al. 2016; Martinez et al. 2020; Martinez,

Amson, et al. 2023; T. D. Smith, Eiting, and Bhatnagar 2012; Herbert et al. 2018) as well as a

dual function (e.g., T. D. Smith et al. 2007; 2016; Pang et al. 2016; Yee et al. 2016; Martinez et

al. 2020; Martinez, Amson, et al. 2023). Despite complex variation in the specific distribution of

epithelium on the nasoturbinal and ethmoturbinal I, we tested each hypothesis of turbinal

functional partitioning and found similar results, which suggests that different assumptions of

epithelial distribution do not have a significant effect on the comparison of olfactory performance

at the interspecific level. Further research should attempt to assess the distribution of epithelium

on the posterior transverse lamina, the mesethmoid, and the walls that bound and face into the

nasal cavity across a wide range of taxa, since these structures have also been identified from

histological stains as containing olfactory and respiratory epithelium (Barrios et al., 2014;

Macrini, 2014; Rowe et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2011).

While myrmecophagous and non-myrmecophagous species were discriminated in the

morphospace, our morphometric results primarily separated groups based on taxonomic order

rather than dietary specialization (Fig. 8). Comparison of functional turbinal surface area and

functional 3D complexity between groups revealed no significant separation between

myrmecophagous and non-myrmecophagous species (Table 6). Such an absence of difference

between the olfactory turbinals of myrmecophagous and non-myrmecophagous mammals does

not necessarily indicate that myrmecophagous mammals have similar olfactory capabilities than

non-myrmecophagous mammals. In fact, the establishment of a link between diet and the

surface area of the olfactory turbinals or their olfactory epithelium has been rarely tested

(Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Martinez et al., 2018; Melin et al., 2022; Valkenburgh et al.,

2014; Yohe et al., 2022), and the relation between olfactory turbinals, their genomics proxies, as

well as with olfactory capabilities has been questioned (Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Martinez,

Courcelle, et al., 2023). Increased size of the olfactory recess slows down airflow in the olfactory


<!-- Page 30 -->


region during both inspiration and expiration, allowing odorants to recirculate within the olfactory

recess (Eiting et al., 2014). Turbinal morphology and complexity may also function to redirect

airflow in the nasal cavity, as has been demonstrated in canids (Craven et al., 2007, 2010).

Sniffing may also allow more air (and odor molecules) to enter the olfactory recess and circulate

around and between turbinal bones (Rygg et al., 2017). A study investigating turbinal

morphology among rodents identified increased 3D complexity of olfactory turbinals in species

specialized for feeding primarily on underground earthworms, where higher olfactory sensitivity

capabilities might be required (Martinez et al., 2018). More complex fractal-like turbinals in one

region might cause differential circulation throughout the nasal cavity, which leads to adaptive

responses without changes to the total surface area of a structure. If olfactory capabilities are

primarily driven by the amount of epithelium, measures of surface area should capture most of

the variation in performance. Instead, if redirecting airflow improves olfactory capabilities without

increasing the amount of epithelium, surface area may not be as important as bone shape. In

the latter scenario, 3D complexity may better approximate olfactory function with similar

performance being potentially achievable through different morphologies. Performance tests

should be conducted for each investigated species to properly characterize potential differences

in olfactory function and link them to differences in olfactory shape and complexity.

Several myrmecophagous species are known to spend a significant amount of time

underground (Nowak, 2018; Wilson & Mittermeier, 2009, 2011). In rodents, subterranean

lifestyles increase hypoxia and hypercapnia, generating additional physiological stresses during

ventilation not faced by their surface dwelling counterparts (Lacey & Patton, 2000). All

myrmecophagous species are also characterized by a lower basal metabolic rate compared to

most placental species (McNab, 1980). The maxilloturbinal is covered by a respiratory

epithelium that functions to conserve heat (Hillenius, 1992; Schmidt-Nielsen et al., 1970).

Reduced metabolic activity may require more respiratory epithelium to heat incoming air during


<!-- Page 31 -->


inspiration, corresponding to an enlarged maxilloturbinal. We found no significant differences in

respiratory turbinal surface area or complexity between myrmecophagous and non-

myrmecophagous species. Ratios of olfactory to respiratory surface area proved to be

challenging to interpret here as higher ratios might result from the development of olfactory

turbinals rather than a reduction of respiratory ones. In theory, lower demand for

thermoregulatory capability would require less respiratory epithelium and might explain a

reduction in maxilloturbinal size. Such reduction was particularly pronounced in the

maxilloturbinal of D. novemcinctus and D. pilosus. Because armadillos live in burrows, they are

subject to overheating and may have evolved carapaces with high minimum thermal

conductance to adapt to the environment (McNab, 1980). A reduced need for thermoregulation

may have played a role in the reduction in size of the maxilloturbinal in these armadillos, but the

giant armadillo (P. maximus) also possesses a carapace and is not characterized by a reduced

maxilloturbinal. Moreover, the role of the maxilloturbinal in thermal biology may not be as crucial

as previously thought, with neither corrected basal metabolic rate nor body temperature being

significantly correlated with the relative surface area of the maxilloturbinal at a mammalian scale

(Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al., 2023). Here again, myrmecophagous species demonstrate that

establishing a direct link between turbinal morphology and function can prove challenging,

especially in understudied taxa.

Morphological Convergence Among Myrmecophagous Mammals

The morphology of anteaters and pangolins is strikingly similar to the extent that

taxonomists have previously suggested that they shared a direct common ancestor (Paulli,

1900; Wilson & Mittermeier, 2011). Molecular studies have shown that pangolins are instead

more closely related to carnivorans, suggesting that similarities between anteater and pangolin

morphology are the result of convergence (Delsuc et al., 2002; Meredith et al., 2011; Murphy et


<!-- Page 32 -->


al., 2001). Ferreira-Cardoso et al. (2019) demonstrated that convergent tooth loss resulted in

divergent internal structures of the mandible of anteaters and pangolins despite the superficial

resemblance of their masticatory apparatus (Ferreira-Cardoso et al., 2019). Here, we found that

variation in turbinal morphology is explained more strongly by taxonomic order (p = 0.001, r2 =

0.576) than by dietary specialization to myrmecophagy (p = 0.023, r2 = 0.101), which reflects

species distribution in the morphospace. In the morphospace, no PC separates anteaters and

pangolins from the remaining species, and these two groups occupy minimally overlapping

regions of the morphospace (Fig. 8). In particular, anteaters, except Cy. didactylus, occupy the

maximum values along PC1 corresponding primarily to the elongated maxilloturbinals and

nasoturbinals. Surface area and 3D complexity are unable to separate anteaters and pangolins

from their sister taxa (Table 6). The main observable similarity among these species is an

enlarged semicircular lamina (Figs. 3, 4, and S1). The semicircular lamina is generally covered

by olfactory epithelium but because some variation exists among mammals, its exact function

remains unclear (Martinez, Amson, et al., 2023; Smith & Bonar, 2022).

However, our detailed comparative descriptions suggest morphological convergence

between the giant armadillo (P. maximus) and the aardvark (O. afer). The turbinals in these two

species are complex, filigree scrolls that are interwoven and interlocked. They are relatively

large in body size and dramatically different from the other species included in this study. P.

maximus and O. afer display the highest number of combined ethmoturbinal and frontoturbinal

counts, with 47 and 40, respectively (Table 5). However, they differ in the distribution of these

turbinals, with O. afer showing an unusual higher number of frontoturbinals compared to

ethmoturbinals. The caudal portion of ethmoturbinal I in these two species is also very complex

in comparison to all other species examined, with many attachment sites to the cribriform plate

and posterior transverse lamina. O. afer and P. maximus appeared similar in that their

ethmoturbinals and frontoturbinals each exhibit exceptional complexity (Fig. 9). These two


<!-- Page 33 -->


species generally occupy regions of the morphospace with increased PC2 values,

corresponding to relatively constant ventrodorsal height of the turbinal complex from rostral to

caudal ends (e.g., contrast with B. tridactylus) (Fig. 8). However, there are many species with

high PC2 values, suggesting this axis of variation is not primarily associated with the unique

similarities between O. afer and P. maximus (Fig. 8). It is possible that generating morphospace

data using Type II landmarks, which were necessary here given the complex nature of turbinal

shape but are generally not as reliable indicators of homology as Type I landmarks, is not

capturing shape information that could distinguish these two species from the rest of the taxa.

Similarities between the surface area and complexity match with the significant correlation

between respiratory turbinal complexity and surface area found in rodents (Martinez et al., 2018;

Martinez, Okrouhlík, et al., 2023). The entire internal nasal system of these species may be

converging to a morphology different from other myrmecophagous mammals. These two

species are highly fossorial (Superina & Loughry, 2012; Taylor et al., 2002) and build burrows to

forage (Abba et al., 2005), although these ecological characteristics are also found in other

armadillos, which are not included in this study such as naked-tailed armadillos (Cabassous

ssp.) and fairy armadillos (Chlamyphorus truncatus and Calyptophractus retusus). However, the

burrows of P. maximus and O. afer are quite unique in their depth, so that they are considered

as burrowing ecosystem engineers (Desbiez & Kluyber, 2013; Louw et al., 2019). Furthermore,

these two species are known for spending much less time aboveground than other

myrmecophagous mammals (Nowak, 2018; Wilson & Mittermeier, 2011). In subterranean

rodents, odor discrimination has been demonstrated to be a method for identifying and

subsequently orienting digging towards edible plants (Heth et al., 2002; Heth & Todrank, 2007).

Increased size and complexity of olfactory structures are present in subterranean animals

ranging from cave-dwelling fish (Soares & Niemiller, 2013) to troglobitic beetles (Balart-García

et al., 2021). While the connection between modified structure and precise olfactory function

needs further research to elucidate, it is a reasonable explanation that reduced vision in dark


<!-- Page 34 -->


subterranean environments may be associated with increased reliance on olfactory or other

sensory capabilities across animals broadly. Although the structure and numbers of ethmo- and

frontoturbinals clearly diverged, the overall increased complexity and surface area of the

turbinals in these two species might relate to similarities in underground lifestyle, perhaps by

modifying turbinal morphology for odorants to circulate longer near the olfactory epithelium in

order to increase the chance of detection while underground. Maintaining efficient gas exchange

creates an additional physiological stress in hypoxic and hypercapnic conditions (Lacey &

Patton, 2000), which may explain why respiratory turbinals are more complex in addition to the

olfactory turbinals in these two fossorial and burrowing species.

As aardwolves have a very specific diet feeding almost exclusively on termites (Cooper &

Skinner, 1979; De Vries et al., 2011), we expected that their olfactory system might have shown

strong modifications for scent discrimination compared to closely related carnivorous hyaenids.

Among carnivorans, ethmoturbinal I extends furthest rostrally in the myrmecophagous southern

aardwolf (P. cristatus) (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Plates). Compared to its sister taxa, the

striped hyaena (H. hyaena), P. cristatus possesses extended ethmoturbinals and

frontoturbinals, which reflect the elongation of the snout found in other myrmecophagous

mammals (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Plates). Such elongation of the snout is also represented

in the morphospace (Fig. 8), with P. cristatus being set apart from other carnivorans. P. cristatus

has also a large ratio of olfactory to respiratory surface areas (Supplementary Figure S2).

However, it is difficult to draw clear conclusions from these observations. Indeed, olfaction is a

broad term that encompasses several different specific functions, such as detecting odorants at

low concentrations (sensitivity), discriminating between similar odors, or perceiving a wide range

of odorant molecules (Martinez, Courcelle, et al., 2023; Valkenburgh et al., 2014). Specific

olfactory functions may thus be advantageous in different ecological contexts. The aardwolf (P.

cristatus) scrapes dirt over its feces, and it has been hypothesized that this behavior helps to


<!-- Page 35 -->


mask the terpene scent of the termites, possibly to avoid olfactory confusion of feces with

Trinervitermes feeding columns (Kruuk & Sands, 1972; Richardson, 1990). Such behavior could

reflect an increased sensitivity to terpene odorants produced by this specific termite genus

(Richardson & Levitan, 1994). With a lifestyle so focused on detecting the odorants produced by

Trinervitermes, P. cristatus may be more effective at discriminating between odors than

perceiving a wide range of odorant molecules, as might be necessary for the more generalist

anteaters and pangolins.

## Conclusion

Surface area, 3D complexity metrics, and geometric morphometric results provide further

evidence that the difference between turbinals in myrmecophagous and non-myrmecophagous

species is minimal compared to the extent to which phylogeny shaped the evolution of these

structures. Our comparative descriptions showed that the turbinal complexity in shape and

numbers represents a potentially interesting source of morphological data for future

phylogenetic systematics studies. Convergence in external traits such as snout length does not

equate to convergence in the underlying internal skeleton structures. However,

myrmecophagous species that spend a lot of time underground in their burrows (O. afer and P.

maximus) have distinctly similar turbinal counts and complexity that may correspond to

increased reliance on olfaction, though further research is needed to elucidate the precise

relationship between structure and function in these species. The aardwolf (P. cristatus) also

displays a modified olfactory system, which might relate to its extreme dietary specialization to

detect the odorant of termites they exclusively feed on. In contrast, the anteaters and pangolins

are more generalists and live above ground, and their turbinals may not be as constrained by

odor sensitivity or discrimination. Olfaction is complex and consists of many underlying functions

that are commonly described as a single sense. The nuance of describing differences in


<!-- Page 36 -->


olfaction should not be lost, and myrmecophagous mammals will provide an excellent system

for exploring these form-function relationships.
